title: Motor Neurone Disease: End-of-Life Anticipatory Prescribing

evidenceAudit.scope: End-of-life planning and anticipatory medicines for adults with motor neurone disease (MND) using NICE NG42, with doses from the Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines last-days page and NHS Lanarkshire non-invasive ventilation withdrawal guidance.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: NICE NG42 names the medicine classes for anticipatory prescribing but gives no doses; doses come from general last-days-of-life guidance, not MND-specific guidance.
The issuing body and review date of the Scottish symptom-control page were not stated in the page text opened.
The NHS Lanarkshire document states that withdrawal of ventilation in MND differs and refers to external guidance that was not opened.
Renal-impairment dosing is not given in the sources opened.
No Saudi MND or palliative prescribing guideline was opened; SFDA registration was not verified.
Doses are for adults; specialist palliative advice is required for opioid-tolerant patients and for terminal agitation.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Worsening respiratory impairment causes breathlessness; a raised arterial carbon dioxide level triggers urgent referral to a respiratory ventilation service. Excess saliva, thick secretions and an ineffective cough are managed separately with antimuscarinics, secretion measures and cough augmentation. Anxiety makes breathlessness worse, so a benzodiazepine can be added to an opioid. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) can relieve symptoms but some people depend on it 24 hours a day, so stopping it needs a symptom plan. Communication, cognition or capacity may decline, so advance care planning should start early.

symptoms: Distress or fear as the end of life approaches.
physicalSigns: Resting oxygen saturation at or below 92% with known lung disease, or at or below 94% without it, prompting blood gas analysis.
redFlags: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) above 6 kPa: refer urgently to a respiratory ventilation service, to be seen within 1 week.
A significant change in respiratory function: offer an end-of-life discussion.
A person using NIV continuously who wishes to stop, or who becomes distressed when it is stopped.
Symptoms not controlled with first-line anticipatory medicines: seek specialist palliative care advice.
precipitants: Respiratory tract infection or secretion retention (reversible causes to treat first).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Treat infection and secretion problems before attributing breathlessness to disease progression.
Breathlessness is made worse by anxiety; a benzodiazepine is considered.
Excess saliva responds to an antimuscarinic; thick secretions need medicines review, hydration, suction, humidification or carbocisteine.

clinicalManagement.title: Plan before the terminal phase
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and at each trigger point
actions: Offer end-of-life discussion at diagnosis, before gastrostomy or NIV, and when respiratory function changes significantly.
Cover advance care planning, advance decisions to refuse treatment, do-not-attempt-cardiopulmonary-resuscitation (DNACPR) orders, lasting power of attorney and anticipatory medicines at home.
Start earlier if communication, cognition or capacity is expected to fall.

clinicalManagement.title: Have anticipatory medicines and equipment ready
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before breathlessness or distress becomes severe
actions: Ensure prompt access to an opioid and a benzodiazepine for breathlessness, and an antimuscarinic for saliva and secretions.
Ensure access to specialist palliative care, a communication aid and equipment such as syringe drivers and suction.
Consider as-needed breathlessness medicines at home for people using NIV.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat symptoms in the last days
actions: Breathlessness, opioid-naive: morphine 2 mg SC as needed, maximum 6 doses in 24 hours; add midazolam 2–5 mg SC up to hourly for breathlessness with anxiety.
Persistent breathlessness: morphine 5–10 mg SC and midazolam 5–20 mg SC over 24 hours by syringe pump.
Secretions: hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg SC up to hourly (maximum 120 mg in 24 hours); second line glycopyrronium 200 micrograms SC 6–8 hourly as needed.
Seek urgent advice if 3 or more doses within 4 hours give little benefit; seek advice or review if more than 6 doses are needed in 24 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: If NIV is to be stopped
actions: Agree the decision with the person and, if they wish, family; involve clinicians with NIV-withdrawal expertise and check legal and ethical frameworks.
Have DNACPR in place and symptoms controlled first; start a continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI) of an opioid and midazolam at least 2 hours before withdrawal, ideally 4–6 hours (NHS Lanarkshire).
Be ready to give repeated as-needed doses before and after withdrawal.

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG42 recommends having an opioid, a benzodiazepine and an antimuscarinic available but gives no doses. Doses below are from the Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines last-days page (general, not MND-specific). Check hospital formulary and specialist palliative advice; SFDA registration was not verified.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Current or anticipated significant or complex needs (Rec 1.5.11).
Diagnosis, need for gastrostomy or NIV, or a significant change in respiratory function (Rec 1.7.1).
Resting room-air oxygen saturation at or below 92% with known lung disease, or at or below 94% without (Rec 1.15.11).
PaCO2 above 6 kPa, to be seen within 1 week (Rec 1.15.13).

teaching.scope: End-of-life planning and anticipatory medicines for adults with motor neurone disease (MND) using NICE NG42, with doses from the Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines last-days page and NHS Lanarkshire non-invasive ventilation withdrawal guidance.
learningObjectives: Start end-of-life planning at the trigger points.
Prescribe anticipatory medicines for breathlessness, distress and secretions.
pitfalls: Waiting until the last days to discuss end of life.
Using general last-days doses without specialist advice in opioid-tolerant patients.
Withdrawing NIV before symptoms are controlled.
keyPoints: NG42 names the medicine classes but not the doses.
PaCO2 above 6 kPa needs ventilation-service review within 1 week.
Start the CSCI at least 2 hours before NIV withdrawal.

patientEducation: Explain that NIV can be stopped at any time and that medicines can ease symptoms.
Explain expected changes at the end of life to family and carers.
lifestyleAndDiet: Maintain oral care, hydration, upright posture and suction to manage saliva and secretions.
mdtReferrals: MND specialist team; specialist palliative care; respiratory ventilation service; speech and language therapy for secretions and communication; community nursing for syringe drivers.
dischargeCriteria: Anticipatory medicines, prescription chart and syringe-driver support in place at home.
Advance care plan, DNACPR and lasting power of attorney documented and shared with GP and emergency services.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review the plan and symptom control at least at each trigger point; respiratory function tests usually every 2 to 3 months; offer bereavement support to family and carers.
